analysis.one_liner: Invests heavily in affordable housing, aids first-time buyers in formerly redlined areas, and raises the estate tax to pay for it.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 14 House Democrats, never received a hearing or a vote and died in committee when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have poured tens of billions of dollars a year into building and preserving affordable rental housing, rewarded local governments that cut zoning barriers, and given down payment grants to first-time homebuyers in neighborhoods that were redlined or racially segregated by law. It also barred Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and HUD from bulk-selling foreclosed homes to investors unless most went to owner-occupants, expanded fair housing protections, and strengthened the Community Reinvestment Act. To pay for it, the bill raised estate and gift taxes on the largest inheritances. It was referred to four House committees and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income renters and first-time homebuyers, especially residents of formerly redlined neighborhoods, who would receive down payment grants and benefit from a large expansion of affordable housing supply; tenants facing eviction, who would gain access to counsel and just-cause protections where local governments adopt them; and Native American and rural housing programs, which would see funding restored and expanded.

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes $44.5 billion a year for the federal Housing Trust Fund and $2.5 billion a year for the Capital Magnet Fund through FY2031 to build and preserve affordable rental housing [S3].

Creates down payment grants for first-time homebuyers in areas graded 'hazardous' or 'definitely declining' by the Home Owners' Loan Corporation, in formerly racially segregated areas, or in concentrated areas of poverty [S3].

Provides $4 billion to a Middle Class Housing Emergency Fund for housing construction and anti-displacement measures including legal representation for tenants facing eviction, with Davis-Bacon prevailing wages on financed construction and affordability in perpetuity for units below 120% of area median income [S3].

Requires HUD to sell at least 75% of foreclosed homes it takes back to owner-occupants or nonprofits, and restricts Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac non-performing loan sales so at least 90% of foreclosed properties go to owner-occupants or affordable rental use, with borrowers getting 90 days' notice and loss mitigation review before any loan sale [S3].
Grants states and localities $2 billion a year to remove zoning barriers, legalize denser housing, and adopt tenant protections such as just-cause eviction and access to counsel [S3].
Expands the Fair Housing Act to bar discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity, marital status, source of income, veteran status, or perceived membership in a protected class [S2].

Appropriates $2.5 billion for Indian Housing Block Grants, $20 million for Native Hawaiian housing, and roughly $500 million for rural housing programs in FY2022, and expands VA home loan eligibility for certain descendants of veterans [S3].

Strengthens the Community Reinvestment Act by covering nonbank mortgage lenders, requiring community benefits plans for bank mergers, and adding public data collection on consumer lending and deposits [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large estates and wealthy heirs, through a restructured estate tax with fewer brackets, higher rates, and a lower basic exemption, plus new limits on estate-planning trusts; banks and nonbank mortgage lenders, which face expanded Community Reinvestment Act obligations and data reporting; and investors who buy foreclosed homes or distressed mortgage loans in bulk, whose volume and resale flexibility would be restricted.

drawbacks.text: The estate tax restructuring is the funding engine but is also the bill's most contested element; Congress has repeatedly cut the estate tax since 2001, so raising rates and lowering the exemption would face immediate opposition from affected families and their representatives, and the bill's massive spending is politically dependent on it [S2].

The bill relies on roughly $50 billion a year in new authorizations, including $44.5 billion annually to the Housing Trust Fund through FY2031, spending on a scale that even housing-focused lawmakers did not advance through the annual appropriations process in this Congress [S3].

Restricting HUD, Fannie Mae, and Freddie Mac sales of foreclosed homes and distressed loans to owner-occupants and nonprofits could reduce the proceeds those agencies recover, a cost that can fall indirectly on taxpayers and on the mortgage insurance funds the sales are meant to protect [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary households locked out of homeownership and for renters facing rising rents, the potential gains are large: a sustained supply subsidy, direct down payment help, and eviction protections. The costs fall on a narrow set of concentrated interests—large estates, banks, and mortgage investors—rather than being spread broadly, though the sheer scale of the spending and the reliance on estate tax increases are the bill's main design vulnerabilities, and the restrictions on distressed-loan sales could recover less money for the government. On balance the trade is a substantial benefit to working and middle-income households at the expense of concentrated wealth.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees the day it was introduced, picked up two subcommittee referrals, and never received a markup or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced April 22, 2021 by Rep. Emanuel Cleaver with 10 original cosponsors including Reps. Khanna, Norton, Pressley, and Schakowsky, and referred to the Financial Services, Judiciary, Veterans' Affairs, and Ways and Means committees [S1,S3].
The full cosponsor list grew to 13, all Democrats; no Republican cosponsored the bill [S4].

On July 14, 2021 it was referred to the Veterans' Affairs Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity, and on October 19, 2021 to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties; no committee ever reported it [S5].
No hearing, markup, or vote is recorded on the bill's action history through the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and mortgage lenders, bulk buyers of foreclosed homes and distressed loans, and holders of the largest estates all kept the status quo; no new affordable housing programs, down payment grants, or estate tax changes took effect.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized the original cosponsor group.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; it had no Republican cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 sponsors were Democrats, there were no Republican cosponsors, and no floor or committee vote ever occurred.

industries.note: Expanded Community Reinvestment Act coverage, mandatory community benefits plans for mergers, and consumer lending data requirements would raise compliance obligations; the counterpart benefit flows to low-income borrowers and communities.

industries.industry: Investors in foreclosed homes and distressed mortgage loans
industries.note: Requirements that 75-90% of foreclosed properties go to owner-occupants or nonprofits, anti-flipping rules on land installment contracts, and borrower notice and loss mitigation protections would shrink their deal flow and resale options.

industries.industry: Large estates and estate planning professionals
industries.note: Higher estate tax rates, a lower exemption, and new limits on grantor trusts and generation-skipping trusts would raise taxes on the largest inheritances; this is the bill's revenue source.
Tens of billions in Housing Trust Fund, Capital Magnet Fund, and emergency fund dollars would flow through states, nonprofits, and housing finance agencies to build and preserve affordable units.

industries.industry: Homebuilders and local real estate markets
industries.note: Grants rewarding zoning reform and denser building would expand construction opportunities, while restrictions on bulk foreclosure sales could shift some inventory away from investor buyers toward owner-occupants.
